lesson.title: Turn a calculation into a tool

lead.text: Here is the till card as Python: def cost(units): return units * 5. This is a function, a piece of code with a name, written once and run whenever it is needed. The first line starts with def and gives the function its name, cost, then lists in brackets what it needs. Each name in the brackets is a parameter, a label for a value the function will be given. Here there is one, units. The indented line underneath is the body, the work done every time the function runs.

Using the function is called calling it. You write its name with the values in brackets, as in cost(3). The value you pass is the argument, and Python attaches it to the parameter, so inside that call units stands for 3. The word return sends an answer back to the place that made the call. cost(3) hands back 15, and total = cost(3) stores that 15 under the name total. The parameter is the label inside the function, and the argument is the actual value from outside. Calling cost(8) afterwards gives the same rule a new argument and a new answer.

Many people expect a function to show its answer on the screen, and print does that. print writes text for a person to read. return does a different job: it hands a value back to the code that called the function, where it can be stored and used in more arithmetic. A function can print, return or do both. Each has its own effect. Step through the picture, where one function returns twice its input and another only prints it.

afterFigure.text: The first function returns 8, so result holds 8. The second prints 8 on the screen, but nothing is returned, so result holds None. None is Python's value for 'nothing here', and a function that finishes without reaching a return line hands it back. The 8 on the screen was shown to the reader and stored nowhere. If a later line needs the answer, the function has to return it.

cases.label: Case A

lead.text: The parameter x receives the argument. Follow it through the body to the line that sends the answer back.
Showing a number and giving it back are separate jobs. Decide what the caller receives when only the first is done.

The till card said the rate is 5 unless the card says otherwise. A function can follow the same rule with a default, a value a parameter takes when the call leaves it out. In def cost(units, rate=5): return units * rate, the parameter rate has a default of 5. So cost(3) leaves rate alone and gets 15. A call such as cost(3, 7) fills both parameters: values given by position go to the parameters in order, so rate becomes 7 and the answer is 21.

An argument can also be given by name, which is called a keyword argument. In cost(rate=7, units=3) each value is labelled with the parameter it fills, so the order no longer matters. The name tells Python where each value goes. Names also make a call easier to read when several values look alike. Step through the picture and compare a call that uses the default with one that names both values.

afterFigure.text: The first call uses the default rate of 5 and gives 15. The second replaces the rate with 7 and gives 21. Both run the same function, and only the arguments changed.

steps.headline: With def pay(hours, wage=10): return hours * wage, what do pay(3) and pay(wage=12, hours=2) give?

lead.text: Check both ways of passing values on one small function.

workedSteps.text: pay(3) gives hours the value 3. No wage is passed, so the default 10 is used.

steps.headline: With def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate, what does cost(rate=6, units=5) return?

workedSteps.text: Keywords name the parameters. So units is 5 and rate is 6.
Multiply the two. What does cost return?

lead.text: So far the arguments have been numbers, and a number cannot be changed in place. A list can be, and that raises a new question: what does a function do to a list it is handed? Python does not copy the list into the function. The parameter becomes another name for the same list the caller holds, much as two labels can point at one locker.

That gives two different outcomes. A method such as append changes the list itself, so def add_item(items): items.append(9) changes the caller's list, and the caller sees the 9 afterwards. An assignment such as items = [9] only points the name items at a new list. The caller's list is left as it was, because only a label inside the function moved. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: In the first case values goes from [1, 2] to [1, 2, 9] after the call. In the second it stays [1, 2]. When you read any function, ask whether it changes the object it was given or only points its own label somewhere else.

lead.text: Find the line that changes the list, then decide how many items the caller's list holds afterwards.

Not every rule has to be written by you. Python ships with a large stock of ready-made functions, grouped into modules, which are files of related code. The word import loads a module. After import math, its functions are reached through the module's name: math.sqrt(81) is 9.0, and math.ceil(4.2) is 5, because ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

Typing a long module name over and over gets tiring, so import allows an alias, a shorter name of your choosing. import math as m makes m.ceil(4.2) the same call as math.ceil(4.2). The alias exists only inside your program. The rest of this course imports NumPy as np in the same way. One limit is worth knowing. import loads a module that is already installed. It cannot fetch a missing package from the internet, so importing something that is not installed stops the program with an error.
Treat the alias as one more name for the same module, and work out what the call returns.

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import math as m
result = m.sqrt(81)

blocks.text: A card taped beside the till reads: cost = units × rate, where the rate is 5 pounds a unit unless the card says otherwise. Everyone who serves a customer follows it the same way. They take the number of units, multiply it by the rate and say the total. Nothing on the card has to be remembered, and nobody invents their own version.

The barrier program from the last lesson needed a fee rule too, and so do the shop's stock sheet and its website. Copying the arithmetic into each place works until the rate changes, and then one copy always gets forgotten. The card has the right idea. The rule is written once and given a name, and every place that needs it refers to the name.

Python lets you do exactly that. This lesson turns the till card into a named rule. It looks at what comes back from the rule and what happens when a value is missing. It also covers what a rule can do to the things it is handed. It ends by borrowing rules that other people have already written.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a function call and tell what return gives back that print does not.

recap.keyIdea: A function takes arguments through its parameters and hands a value back with return; print only displays, and import makes a module's names available.

blocks.text: You priced a 3-unit sale at £15 with the default rate, called triple(7) for 21 and found that cost(rate=6, units=5) gives 30. You also saw that a function which only prints hands back None, and that m.ceil(4.2) rounds up to 5.

recap.nextHook: Every rule so far was handed values it could use. Real data is less tidy. A form that asks for an age will sometimes come back with the word 'unknown', and int('unknown') stops a program dead. The next lesson shows how to expect that failure, carry on past it and say how much you skipped.

questions.prompt: def triple(x): return x * 3. What does triple(7) return?
hints: Put the argument in place of the parameter.
The parameter x receives the argument 7.
Apply the multiplication by 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The argument 7 is multiplied by 3 and returned as 21.

questions.onCorrect: 21. The argument 7 went into x, and return sent x * 3 back.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the argument. The function returns the argument multiplied by 3.

hints: Match each keyword to its parameter name.
units is 5 and rate is 6.
Multiply the two values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Keyword arguments assign units = 5 and rate = 6, so the product is 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. The keywords set units to 5 and rate to 6, replacing the default rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the default rate 4. Here rate=6 replaces it.
That adds the values. The function multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A function prints 12 but has no return statement. What does the call return?
hints: Think about the value handed to the caller, not the text shown on screen.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Printing and returning are separate. A function that reaches the end without return produces None.

questions.onCorrect: None. Printing shows text, while a function with no return statement hands back None.

misconceptions.feedback: 12 was displayed, not handed back. The call itself returns None.
return is a keyword, not a value. Without it, the call gives None.

questions.prompt: After import math as m, what is m.ceil(4.2)?
hints: m is the alias for the math module.
ceil rounds up, not to the nearest.
Which whole number is just above 4.2?
questions.onCorrect: 5. m is the math module under a short name, and ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds down. ceil rounds up.

questions.prompt: def cost(units, rate=4): return units * rate. What does cost(8) return?
hints: Use the default for the missing argument.
No rate was passed.
Multiply the units by the default rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The omitted rate uses the default 4: 8 × 4 = 32.

questions.onCorrect: 32. The omitted rate takes its default of 4, so the call computes 8 × 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the default rate. The function multiplies.
That ignores the rate. The default 4 still multiplies.

hints: Find the non-negative square root.
A square root reverses squaring.
Which whole number multiplied by itself gives 144?
questions.onCorrect: 12. The square root reverses squaring, and 12 × 12 is 144.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves 144. A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to give it.

hints: Which line gives a value back to the caller?
print only writes the text on screen.
Work out what return sends back for x = 3.
questions.prompt: def f(x): print(x); return x + 1. After y = f(3), what number does y hold?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The function prints 3 and returns 3 + 1 = 4, so y holds 4.

questions.onCorrect: 4. print showed 3 on screen, but only return decides what y holds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was printed. y holds what return sent back.

hints: Which rate applies when the card says nothing else?
The cost multiplies units by the rate.
Work out 3 × 5.
questions.prompt: What does 3 units cost, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 units at the default rate 5 cost 15.

questions.onCorrect: £15. The default rate of 5 applies unless you say otherwise. A default argument works exactly this way.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds units and rate. The card says units × rate.
That is the number of units. Multiply by the rate.

hints: How does Python know which value is the wage?
questions.prompt: Why does the order of the two arguments not matter here?

choices.label: Each keyword names the parameter it fills

acceptedIdeas: Each keyword names the parameter it fills
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keyword arguments name their parameters, so Python can match them in any order.

questions.onCorrect: Each keyword names the parameter it fills, so position does not matter.

misconceptions.feedback: The product comes out the same either way, but the reason is the keywords.
Python uses the names to choose which parameter each value fills.

hints: Does the parameter refer to the caller's list or to a copy?
append changes the object it is called on.
Start with the original items and add two.
questions.prompt: def grow(items): items.append(7); items.append(8). With values = [1, 2, 3, 4] and the call grow(values), what is len(values)?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The function appends two items to the caller's list, so it now has six.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The parameter and values refer to one list, so both appends are visible to the caller.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the original length. The parameter names the same list, so the appends show in values.
